title: Museum of Modern Art: Masterpieces
subtitle: Twenty works that change the rules for bodies, objects and painted space.
introduction:
A soup can repeats thirty-two times. A bed stands upright against a wall. Clocks soften, a rubber glove shares a setting with a classical head, and a sofa appears in a jungle. The ordinary object survives each of these changes; in fact, recognition makes the change more noticeable.

This selection from the Museum of Modern Art follows several ways of disturbing the familiar. Some artists alter a thing's shape, others its company, scale or use. Still others remove recognisable objects altogether and leave colour or the passage of paint to organise attention. These are not successive steps towards one destination. Comparing them shows how many different problems can sit beneath the convenient label of modern art.
visitNote: This selection covers several parts of the collection. Check MoMA’s object pages for current display locations and loans. Matisse’s Dance (I), painted in 1909, is the earlier canvas; the more strongly coloured 1910 version belongs to the Hermitage.

books.title: Pablo Picasso: A Retrospective
books.author: Edited by William Rubin
books.note: MoMA’s digitized Picasso retrospective catalogue places Les Demoiselles d’Avignon among studies and later works. Comparing them makes the painting’s departures from conventional figure drawing easier to follow.

works.title: The Starry Night
works.credit: Vincent van Gogh. The Starry Night. Image: WikiArt. Public domain (WikiArt label). Proportionally resized and JPEG compressed; no crop.
works.description: The town occupies a comparatively small area beneath the turning sky. Van Gogh joins separate stars through repeated curves and rings, giving the darkness between them an activity of its own. The tall cypress connects the foreground with this upper field. The painting's force can be examined in that distribution of space without treating every stroke as a symptom of its maker's life.

works.title: Les Demoiselles d'Avignon
works.credit: Pablo Picasso. The girls of Avignon. WikiArt source label: Public domain US. Proportional resize and JPEG compression; no crop. Source: https://www.wikiart.org/en/pablo-picasso/the-girls-of-avignon-1907
works.description: Five figures face the viewer, but their bodies do not settle into one continuous room or one consistent method of representation. Angular planes break across flesh and surrounding space, while the faces differ sharply in treatment. Picasso keeps the group confrontationally present even as its spatial agreement collapses. Identifying the women does not resolve the incompatible ways in which they are shown.

works.title: The Persistence of Memory
works.credit: Salvador Dalí. The Persistence of Memory. Image: WikiArt. Copyright protected (WikiArt label). Proportionally resized and JPEG compressed; no crop.
works.description: Dalí gives the soft watches precise edges and tangible surfaces. They are easy to recognise and impossible to use as ordinary clocks. The distant cliffs retain a firmer appearance, making the contrast more exact. The picture's uncertainty does not come from vague painting; it comes from recognisable things losing the physical properties on which their familiar functions depend.

works.title: Broadway Boogie Woogie
works.credit: Piet Mondrian. Broadway Boogie Woogie. Image: WikiArt. Public domain (WikiArt label). Proportionally resized and JPEG compressed; no crop.
works.description: Small coloured squares interrupt the yellow grid, preventing the lines from functioning as uninterrupted boundaries. Mondrian keeps the right-angled order but gives it a restless internal pulse. The title associates the work with a city and a musical rhythm; neither requires a literal street scene. Movement can be suggested through the spacing of interruptions on an otherwise still surface.

works.title: The Sleeping Gypsy
works.credit: Henri Rousseau. The Sleeping Gypsy. Image: WikiArt. Public domain (WikiArt label). Proportionally resized and JPEG compressed; no crop.
works.description: The lion leans towards the sleeping woman without completing an attack. Her instrument and vessel remain beside her, sharply identifiable in the open landscape. Rousseau suspends the scene at the point where proximity could mean danger, curiosity or something the image does not explain. The title names the sleeper using the artist's historical wording; it does not make the scene an ethnographic record.

works.title: The Dream
works.credit: Henri Rousseau. The Dream. Image: WikiArt. Public domain (WikiArt label). Proportionally resized and JPEG compressed; no crop.
works.description: The sofa makes this jungle impossible to mistake for an unarranged encounter with nature. Rousseau places a familiar indoor object among oversized leaves, animals and a musician. Each part can be examined clearly, even though the whole resists ordinary explanation. The setting remains persuasive as an invented picture precisely because its details do not need to become plausible geography.

works.title: Campbell's Soup Cans
works.medium: Acrylic with metallic enamel paint on canvas, 32 panels
works.credit: Andy Warhol. Campbell's Soup Cans. WikiArt source label: Andy Warhol Fair Use. Proportional resize and JPEG compression; no crop. Source: https://www.wikiart.org/en/andy-warhol/campbells-soup-cans-1962
works.license: Andy Warhol Fair Use (WikiArt source label)
works.description: The repeated design makes the changing soup varieties conspicuous. These thirty-two canvases were painted by hand, despite their resemblance to printed commercial images. Warhol's original display placed them on shelves like groceries. Repetition therefore does more than produce a pattern: it changes the question from how one can is represented to how almost identical goods acquire their small distinctions.

works.title: One: Number 31, 1950
works.credit: One: Number 31. WikiArt; Jackson Pollock. Proportional resizing and JPEG compression; source frame preserved.
works.description: The loops and threads of paint do not converge on a principal figure. Pollock leaves crossings, breaks and successive layers available across the broad field. Instead of looking through those marks to a depicted object, attention follows their passage over the canvas. The absence of a conventional subject does not remove structure; it relocates structure in the relations among the marks.

works.title: I and the Village
works.credit: Marc Chagall. I and the Village. Image: WikiArt. Public domain (WikiArt label). Proportionally resized and JPEG compressed; no crop.
works.description: The green-faced man and the animal meet eye to eye above small houses and figures. Chagall allows different scales to coexist, while circles and diagonals connect areas that would not fit a single measured space. The exchange between the two large faces gives this displaced world an intimate centre. The village can be present as an association without being reconstructed as a panorama.

works.title: The Song of Love
works.credit: Giorgio de Chirico; WikiArt; Public domain (WikiArt label). Source frame preserved; proportionally resized and JPEG compressed.
works.description: A classical head, rubber glove and green ball occupy a setting whose perspective is easier to understand than its contents. De Chirico withholds the practical reason for their meeting. The train in the distance belongs to another kind of everyday movement, yet does not explain the foreground. The objects' clarity keeps the puzzle specific rather than dissolving it into general dreaminess.

works.title: The City Rises
works.credit: Umberto Boccioni. The City Rises. Image: WikiArt. Public domain (WikiArt label). Proportionally resized and JPEG compressed; no crop.
works.description: The red horse's effort spreads into the strokes surrounding workers and construction. Boccioni makes it difficult to separate a body in motion from the urban activity around it. Edges blur where a more descriptive view might distinguish each task. The city is represented through physical strain rather than through a completed skyline: building is still an action taking place.

works.title: Twittering Machine
works.credit: Paul Klee. Twittering Machine. Image: WikiArt. Public domain (WikiArt label). Proportionally resized and JPEG compressed; no crop.
works.description: The crank gives Klee's birdlike figures a troubling shared mechanism. Their thin, individual bodies remain comic and fragile, but the device suggests that sound or movement could be operated from outside. The drawing never needs to become a workable invention. A few connecting lines are enough to make living creatures and mechanical control occupy the same small structure.

works.title: Abstract Painting, Blue
works.credit: Ad Reinhardt. Abstract Painting (Blue). Image: WikiArt. Copyright protected (WikiArt label). Proportionally resized and JPEG compressed; no crop.
works.description: At first the blue can seem continuous. Subdued rectangles gradually divide it into darker and greenish passages, with no emphatic outline to announce their importance. Reinhardt makes a familiar act of looking for the subject give way to distinguishing neighbouring colours. A reproduction may change those close values, so its apparent simplicity should not be treated as the work's final measure.

works.title: Dance (I)
works.credit: Henri Matisse. Dance (I). Image credit: Henri Matisse; Source credit: MoMA. Public domain (https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/mark/1.0/). Proportional resize and JPEG compression; full source frame retained.
works.description: The reaching hands nearly fail to close the ring. Matisse leaves the setting spare enough for that small gap and the uneven spaces between bodies to carry the movement. Five figures do not become a mechanically repeated pattern. Their connection requires effort, making the circle appear maintained in motion rather than laid out as a finished emblem.

works.title: Actor's Mask
works.medium: Oil on canvas mounted on board
works.credit: Paul Klee. Actor's Mask. Image: WikiArt. Public domain (WikiArt label). Proportionally resized and JPEG compressed; no crop.
works.description: Thin divisions turn the green face into a constructed surface. Eyes and mouth remain sufficient for recognition even when they do not settle into an easy expression. Klee places a person-like image between two categories: a face to be read and an object to be worn. The title keeps performance in view without supplying a character or a story.

works.title: Agapanthus
works.credit: Claude Monet. Agapanthus. Image: WikiArt. Public domain (WikiArt label). Proportionally resized and JPEG compressed; no crop.
works.description: The near flowers and reflected growth share Monet's long, overlapping marks. Clear outlines do not consistently separate plant, water and distance. Recognising the scene requires following changes within the handling rather than finding a boundary around each leaf. The overlapping marks keep that search close to the surface, making the garden less a surveyable place than a densely occupied field of colour.

works.title: Agony
works.credit: Arshile Gorky. Agony. Image: WikiArt. Public domain (WikiArt label). Proportionally resized and JPEG compressed; no crop.
works.description: Gorky's thin contours approach recognisable bodies and fragments without fixing them completely. Red and black shapes gather unevenly against the brownish ground. The title supplies a painful association, but not an illustrated event that can be decoded once and left behind. The painting allows bodily suggestions to persist in forms that remain capable of being read otherwise.

works.title: American Landscape
works.credit: Charles Sheeler. American Landscape. Image: WikiArt. Copyright protected (WikiArt label). Proportionally resized and JPEG compressed; no crop.
works.description: Still water and sharply placed structures give Sheeler's factory complex an unusual composure. The small boat offers a measure against the industrial forms. Unlike Boccioni's construction scene, this view suppresses the strain of operation. The machinery appears settled within a carefully spaced landscape, raising a useful distinction between depicting a place of work and depicting the work performed there.

works.title: Bather
works.credit: Henri Matisse. Bather. Image: WikiArt. Public domain (WikiArt label). Proportionally resized and JPEG compressed; no crop.
works.description: The turned back and large limbs retain bodily weight without elaborate anatomical shading. Matisse assigns much of that work to firm contours and broad blue and green areas. The figure remains physically present even as descriptive detail is reduced. Simplification here can be judged by what it preserves, not merely by counting what has been left out.

works.title: Bed
works.medium: Oil and pencil on pillow, quilt, and sheet on wood supports
works.credit: Robert Rauschenberg. Bed. Image: WikiArt. Copyright protected (WikiArt label). Proportionally resized and JPEG compressed; no crop.
works.description: The pillow, sheet and quilt are actual bedding, not painted imitations. Rauschenberg marks them with oil and pencil and sets them upright on wooden supports. They retain their domestic identity while their new position makes ordinary use impossible. The work does not let the viewer decide comfortably between furnishing and painting; each category continues to interfere with the other.

closingSections.title: Keep the differences in view
paragraphs: Warhol repeats an image of an object; Rauschenberg uses the object itself. Dalí changes physical behaviour; de Chirico changes company. Distinguishing these operations gives more to discuss than calling them all strange. Use the museum's current records for display information: this selection connects ideas and works, not guaranteed stops in a particular installation.
